Rental Income Tax for Non-Resident Landlords: What South Africa Actually Taxes

2026.11.04 12 min read Scott Huang Offshore Property

Cape Town rents are rising faster than most Taiwanese buyers expect. The PayProp rental index for the second quarter of 2026 puts the Cape Town average monthly rent at R12,561, up 9.7% year on year (a rise of R1,107); the Western Cape remains the most expensive province in South Africa, and PayProp commercial director Michelle Dickens attributes the move directly to semigration. Annualised, a Cape Town flat at R12,561 a month produces R150,732 of gross rent.

Three scope points before the numbers. Rental income tax South Africa applies to taxable profit rather than gross rent. Non resident rental income tax South Africa differs from the resident case in filing identity, not in the base. Tax on rental property South Africa is declared on an ITR12 each year, and SARS rental income tax bands start at 18% for the 2026/27 year.

That is not the number you keep. South African rental income tax is levied on profit after allowable expenses, and for a non-resident landlord the filing identity, the expense tests and the Taiwan side are three separate questions. This article does one thing: it works out the tax on the holding period - what the tax base is, which costs genuinely qualify, how a non-resident files, what actually reaches your account, and how this differs from the s35A withholding tax charged when you sell. Every rate carries its source and retrieval date; this is information, not tax advice.

Key takeaway: South African rental income tax is charged on taxable profit, not on gross rent. On the Cape Town average of R12,561 a month, full-year gross rent is R150,732; after one vacant month you collect R138,171, and after R56,917 of rates, levies, insurance, repairs and letting commission the taxable income is R81,254. At the 18% band for the 2026/27 year the tax is R14,626, leaving about R66,628 of cash flow - a net yield of roughly 3.33% on a R2,000,000 flat, against a headline 6.9%. If the R17,820 primary rebate applies, the tax in this example falls to zero - that point must be confirmed by a South African tax adviser against your residence status. Market-reference illustration, not a guaranteed return.

How is South African rental income tax calculated?

South African rental income tax is levied on the taxable profit from letting property, at rates starting at 18% and reaching 45% for the 2026/27 year. The Revenue Service wording is direct: rental income is added to your other income and then reduced by the expenses incurred in producing it; the difference is taxable income. What is taxed is not the R150,732 gross figure but the profit that survives the deductions.

For a Taiwanese owner of a Cape Town flat this has one practical consequence: the rent is not taxed in isolation, it is stacked on top of your other South African source income and taxed at the margin. With one flat and no other South African income the profit sits in the lowest band; with salary, dividends or a second rental in South Africa, the same profit is pushed higher. The South African tax year runs from 1 March to the end of February, not the calendar year.

Taxable income (R)How the tax is computed (2026/27 year)Marginal rate
1 - 245,10018% of taxable income18%
245,101 - 383,100R44,118 + 26% above R245,10026%
383,101 - 530,200R79,998 + 31% above R383,10031%
530,201 - 695,800R125,599 + 36% above R530,20036%
695,801 - 887,000R185,215 + 39% above R695,80039%
887,001 - 1,878,600R259,783 + 41% above R887,00041%
1,878,601 and aboveR666,339 + 45% above R1,878,60045%

Two numbers on the same page are routinely missed: the primary rebate of R17,820 for the 2026/27 year, and the R99,000 threshold for anyone under 65. The rebate is subtracted from the tax once computed, not from the income; the threshold is the level below which a person normally pays no tax. (Source: SARS, Rates of Tax for Individuals, 2027 tax year, retrieved 31 October 2026)

Which expenses can be deducted from rental income?

The Revenue Service allows deductions for rates, bond interest, insurance, repairs, letting commission and levies, but only where the cost produced the rental income. The published list covers rates and taxes, bond interest, advertising, estate agent commission, homeowner insurance (not contents or bond insurance), garden services, repairs to the area actually let, and security and property levies.

What cannot be claimed matters just as much: capital and private expenditure. SARS separates repairs from improvements - restoring a broken geyser to working order is a repair and is deductible, while upgrading a bathroom to a higher specification is an improvement, not deductible against rent, but added to the base cost of the property for capital gains when you sell. Residential letting is also an exempt supply for VAT, so VAT paid on expenses cannot be reclaimed.

ExpenseDeductible against Cape Town rent?Practical note
Property ratesYesUse the municipal account; keep the annual statement
Bond interestYesInterest only, never capital repayment; bank certificate required
Levies and securityYesApplies to sectional title and gated estates
Homeowner insuranceYesBuilding cover only; contents and bond cover excluded
Repairs (restoration)YesMust be distinguishable from an improvement; keep invoices
Letting and managing agent feesYesActual fees charged; contract and statements required
Upgrades and extensionsNoCapital in nature; added to base cost instead

Where only part of the property is let - the common Cape Town arrangement of a main house plus a garden cottage - expenses must be apportioned by area. The official example divides the area let by the total area of the dwelling including garages and outbuildings, then applies that percentage to each expense. For a Cape Town property with a cottage, that ratio decides how much you can claim, and it is the first number a tax adviser will ask for. (Source: SARS, Tax on Rental Income, updated 13 December 2024)

Do non-resident landlords pay tax the same way as locals?

Non-resident rental income is South African source income and must be declared on an ITR12 as a non-resident, with the same taxable-profit base as a local landlord. The difference is not what is taxed but whose income is taxed and how it is declared. A non-resident answers to SARS for South African source income only and does not declare income earned outside South Africa; on the same flat with the same costs, the taxable profit is identical to a resident's.

One mechanism is widely misunderstood: South Africa does not withhold tax on rent the way it does on royalties or interest. Neither the tenant nor the managing agent deducts tax on your behalf. That means you must declare the income yourself or through a representative, and nothing has been set aside when the assessment arrives. In practice provisional tax payments are made twice during the year to avoid a single large settlement.

The document set, in the order Cape Town practice usually demands it: the lease with dates and escalation clauses, twelve months of rent statements, the municipal rates account, the bank's annual interest certificate, the insurance schedule, repair invoices, and the managing agent contract with commission statements. A non-resident also needs an income tax reference number and passport details, plus a signed authority if a representative files on your behalf.

One point to confirm yourself: whether the R17,820 primary rebate applies to a non-resident depends on your residence status and the current interpretation of the law. This article does not decide that question, and cash-flow planning should not assume the rebate is available. Ask a practising South African tax adviser for an opinion on your own facts.

What actually reaches you after tax?

On the Cape Town average rent of R12,561 a month, gross rent is R150,732, expenses of R56,917 leave R81,254 taxable, and 18% tax is R14,626. The table below sets out each layer, assuming a R2,000,000 two-bedroom Cape Town flat, fully deductible bond interest and one vacant month.

LayerAmount (R)Note
Gross rent, 12 months150,732R12,561 x 12, fully let
One vacant month-12,561Two to four weeks is normal in Cape Town long lets
Rent actually collected138,171Tax follows amounts received or accrued
Allowable expenses-56,917Rates 9,600 + levies 18,000 + insurance 6,500 + repairs 9,000 + letting 13,817
Taxable income81,254Falls inside the 18% band
Income tax (before rebate)-14,62681,254 x 18%
After-tax cash flow66,628Before remittance costs and currency movement
Net yield on R2,000,0003.33%Gross rent is 7.54% fully let, 6.91% as collected

The gap between that 3.33% and the headline 7% to 9% quoted for Cape Town comes from three things only: vacancy, expenses and tax. Push taxable income into higher bands and the shape changes - the table below compares three levels under the same rate structure, so you can see which band a second flat would put you in.

This is why, when we look at Cape Town yields, we ask clients to compute after-tax cash flow as a separate column. Gross yield is a screen for choosing an area; after-tax cash flow is what decides whether a second or third property makes sense. (Source: PayProp Q2 2026 rental index, reported by EWN on 18 September 2026)

How does rental tax differ from the s35A withholding on sale?

Rental income tax taxes the profit of the holding period, while s35A withholds from the price at the moment of sale. On the same Cape Town flat you declare rental profit every year while you own it, and when you sell, the buyer's conveyancer withholds a portion of the price and pays it to SARS - 7.5% for a non-resident individual.

ItemRental income tax (holding)s35A withholding (sale)
TimingDeclared annually, recurringOnce, at transfer
BaseRent less allowable expensesSale price, not capital gain
Rate for a non-resident individualProgressive, from 18%7.5% withheld
Who paysThe landlord filesBuyer or conveyancer withholds
Refundable?Reconciled in the annual assessmentAn NR03 application can reduce or waive it

In the year of sale the two overlap: you declare that year's rental profit and also deal with the s35A withholding and an NR03 application. Without an NR03 in place, 7.5% is withheld first and reclaimed later, and for anyone moving the proceeds back to Taiwan that timing gap directly affects the remittance schedule.

Do you pay again in Taiwan on the same rent?

Taiwan counts offshore income in full only once the household total reaches NT$1,000,000 for the year. South African rent of R138,171 converts to roughly NT$266,000 at about ZAR 1 = NT$1.93, well below that threshold, so it is not counted in the basic income amount; the basic-income exemption has been NT$7,500,000 since the 2024 tax year, with any excess taxed at 20% before comparison with ordinary income tax.

On double taxation, the honest position: whether a comprehensive double tax agreement is in force between South Africa and Taiwan must be checked against current SARS and Taiwan Ministry of Finance publications; this article assumes no relief mechanism exists. Without a treaty, South African tax is generally not creditable directly in Taiwan and relief depends on domestic foreign tax credit rules applied case by case. At meaningful amounts, an opinion from both sides before you buy is cheaper than a fix afterwards.

Three practical points. First, Taiwan taxes offshore income, not South African rent, and the two bases differ - South Africa looks at profit after allowable expenses, Taiwan at the offshore income amount. Second, every remittance must be traceable to rent, capital or sale proceeds; using the wrong BOP category does not create extra tax but will stall the payment in compliance review. Third, fix and record the exchange rate date used to convert rent into Taiwan dollars, or the annual filing will not reconcile.

FAQ

Is South African rental tax charged on gross rent or on profit?

On profit. SARS requires rental income to be added to your other income and reduced by the expenses incurred in producing it; rates, bond interest, insurance, repairs, commission and levies all qualify as deductions.

Must a non-resident landlord file in South Africa?

Yes. Rental income is South African source income and must be declared on an ITR12 as a non-resident, with the same taxable-profit base as a resident. South Africa does not withhold tax on rent, so nothing is deducted for you and the return is your responsibility.

What does a R2,000,000 Cape Town flat actually return after tax?

On the average rent of R12,561, one vacant month and R56,917 of allowable expenses, taxable income is R81,254, tax is R14,626 and after-tax cash flow is about R66,628 - a net yield of 3.33%. Market-reference illustration, not a guaranteed return; your result depends on your bond structure and receipts.

Can a non-resident claim the R17,820 primary rebate?

That depends on your residence status and must be confirmed by a practising South African tax adviser; this article does not decide it. If the rebate applies, the tax in the example falls from R14,626 to zero; if not, 18% stands. Plan cash flow on the no-rebate case.

Does rental tax overlap with the s35A withholding when I sell?

They do not double charge, but they meet in the year of sale. Rental tax covers holding-period profit; s35A withholds 7.5% of the price from a non-resident individual at transfer. Apply for an NR03 in advance so the money is not withheld and then reclaimed.

Why handle this through Crestline Advisory?

South African rental tax rarely goes wrong on the rate. It goes wrong on receipts and on filing identity - the same rent, deductible or not, turns on whether the document matches the format SARS accepts.

The three most common failure points

  • Repairs confused with improvements: claiming a new geyser as a repair, or a bathroom upgrade as maintenance, gets both disallowed on review and can reopen earlier years.
  • Expenses not allocated per property: several flats merged into one schedule, or card statements with no invoices, cannot be reconciled line by line at filing time.
  • Filing identity and tax year mismatched: the South African tax year runs March to February, so bookkeeping on a calendar year loses one quarter and adds another every year.

Working through our partner Crestline Advisory (on-the-ground execution in South Africa) means these are checked before filing: each expense mapped to the SARS list, repairs separated from capital spend, non-resident status and tax year corrected, rent and costs filed per property, and a local tax adviser engaged for a formal opinion where needed.
